title: Monster Beverage (Hansen Natural): best US stock of 30 years
body: Hansen's (1935 juice co.) went bankrupt 1988; Rodney Sacks and Hilton Schlosberg bought it and listed it 1990 at pennies. 1990s energy drinks went nowhere; the Monster brand launched 2002 and the company took off. CNBC: ~+200,000% from Feb 1994 to Feb 2024 ($1k -> ~$2m; $55.02 close Feb 2024); ~42% CAGR over the 20 years to 2023 (BusinessTech). Splits 2:1 2005, 4:1 2006, 2:1 2012, 3:1 2016, 2:1 2023 (96x cumulative): a ~$5 2003 Hansen share is ~$0.05 today [split math mine; 2003 price unverified]. Max drawdown: roughly -70% in 2007-08 [unverified]. Growth was overwhelmingly sales/EPS (31 consecutive years of sales growth); P/E rose from low-teens to 30-40x [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2003-05: a tiny company with a new brand growing sales >50%/yr, ~50% gross margins, fully outsourced production (co-packers) and distribution through beer distributors (capital-light), plus action-sports marketing creating a youth category. Coca-Cola's 16.7% stake for >$2bn (2014) and 2015 distribution swap were late confirmation, not the signal. Who caught it: the insiders (Sacks/Schlosberg, large owners); no well-documented famous early outside investor found. Stall: growth slowed to low-teens by 2023-24; stock range-bound ~2021-24. LESSON: a boring-looking small consumer company that creates a category, outsources the capital, and keeps the same owner-managers can compound for decades; the obvious-in-hindsight signal was unit growth + gross margin + zero capex, not a famous holder.

data.early_signals: new brand >50% sales growth, ~50% GM, outsourced bottling + beer-distributor network
data.lesson: category creation + capital-light + owner-managers

title: Netflix 2002-2025: two -75% crashes inside a ~1,000x compounder
body: IPO May 2002 at $15. Splits 2:1 (2004), 7:1 (2015), 10:1 (Nov 17 2025) = 140x, so IPO ~$0.11 on today's basis. Crash 1 (Qwikster): July 2011 peak ~$305 pre-2015-split (~$4.35 today) -> Sept 2012 low ~$53 (~$0.76), about -80%; AP: -75% from mid-July to Dec 2011, $12bn wiped, ~800k-2m subs lost after a ~60% price hike plus the plan to split DVD into 'Qwikster' (reversed in ~3 weeks). Crash 2: Nov 2021 ~$701 (~$70) -> May 2022 ~$163 (~$16), -76%, after the first subscriber loss in a decade. Then password-sharing crackdown + ad tier (ads >50% of signups where offered; ad revenue doubled 2024) -> >300m subs end-2024, stock >$1,000 for most of 2025 (~$110-134 post-split). IPO->2025 peak ~1,000x+; 2012 trough->2025 ~150x+. Rerating split: 2012-21 mostly revenue growth on very high P/E; 2022-25 mostly EPS growth (operating margin ~20% -> ~30%) [margins unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL at each trough: streaming hours and international sub adds kept rising while the stock collapsed; the error was self-inflicted pricing/communication, not demand. Who caught it: Carl Icahn disclosed ~10% in Oct 2012 near the low and made >$1bn [from memory, unverified]. LESSON: when a structurally winning platform crashes on a fixable management error, the drawdown is the opportunity; you must be able to sit through -75% twice.

data.eps_vs_rerating: 2022-25 mostly EPS; P/E compressed in 2022 then partially re-expanded
data.early_signals: engagement/sub growth intact during crashes; errors fixable
data.ended: not ended as of 2025; post-split range
data.lesson: self-inflicted crashes in a winning platform are buyable; survive the drawdown

title: Apple 2003-2012: iPod/iPhone, ~110x with P/E compression
body: Split-adjusted to today's basis (2005 2:1, 2014 7:1, 2020 4:1 = 56x): April 2003 low ~$0.19-0.23 (Statmuse; pre-split ~$13) -> Sept 2012 peak $705 (= $100.72 after 2014 split, ~$25.2 today). ~110x in 9.5 years. In 2003 Apple's market cap (~$5bn) was close to its cash (~$4bn+) [unverified], so the business was priced near zero. Split: this was ALL earnings growth; net income went from ~$69m (FY03) to ~$41.7bn (FY12) while P/E COMPRESSED to ~12-15x by 2012 [figures from memory, unverified]. Max drawdown: Dec 2007 ~$202 -> Jan 2009 ~$78 pre-split (~-61%). EARLY SIGNAL visible in 2003: iTunes Store launch (April 2003) plus iPod for Windows made the iPod a mass product; iPod units and Mac 'halo' gains were reported quarterly; EV ~0. Then the iPhone (2007) and App Store (2008) created platform economics. Who caught it: widely chased by growth funds; no single famous value investor documented here. Ended/stalled: peak Sept 2012, then -44% to ~$385 (Apr 2013) on margin/iPhone 5 fears and a long dead-money spell to 2016. LESSON: a turnaround (Jobs, 1997) plus a new product category can compound EPS 100x+; when the P/E falls while EPS explodes, the multiple was a depressant, not a driver, and the stock still returns 100x.

data.early_signals: iTunes Store + iPod on Windows 2003; market cap ~ cash
data.who_caught_it: growth funds broadly [no documented single name]
data.lesson: EPS can carry 100x even with multiple compression

title: Apple 2016-2023: Berkshire's ~$31bn bet, ~8x as hardware rerated to franchise
body: Berkshire (Combs/Weschler first, then Buffett) started buying in Q1 2016 when Apple traded ~$90-110 pre-2020-split (~$23-27 today) at ~10-11x earnings, ~9x ex-cash, priced as a peaking hardware cyclical after the first iPhone unit decline. Cost: ~$31.1bn for 908m shares (~$34/share avg) per Berkshire. End-2023 ~$198: ~8x from 2016 low, stake worth ~$170bn+. Split [my arithmetic, approx]: EPS ~$2.08 (FY16, adj) -> ~$6.13 (FY23) ≈ 2.9x, helped by ~40% share-count reduction via buybacks; P/E ~11x -> ~30x ≈ 2.8x. So roughly half EPS, half rerating. Drawdowns: Oct 2018-Jan 2019 ~-39%; COVID 2020 ~-31%; 2022 ~-31%. EARLY SIGNAL in 2016: very high retention/upgrade loyalty, Services revenue growing ~20%+ on an installed base >1bn devices, net cash ~$150bn+ funding buybacks, at a market-level multiple. Who caught it: Warren Buffett / Berkshire (documented 13F, letters). Ended: Berkshire sold ~13% in Q1 2024 and ~390m shares in Q2 2024 (~2/3 of stake by late 2024) as P/E reached ~30x with EPS growth single-digit. LESSON: the biggest gain often comes from the market reclassifying a business (cyclical hardware -> consumer franchise/Services toll); once rerated, future returns fall to EPS growth and the same investor may rationally sell.

data.early_signals: 10x P/E, Services growth, installed base, buyback capacity
data.lesson: reclassification rerating; sell discipline when multiple is full

title: Microsoft 2014-2025: Nadella turnaround, $36 -> ~$500+
body: Satya Nadella became CEO Feb 4 2014; stock closed $36.35 that day; market cap ~$300bn; P/E ~13-15x. 'Mobile first, cloud first': Office on iPad (Mar 2014), abandoned the Nokia phone bet (~$7.6bn write-down 2015) [from memory], open-sourced/partnered (Linux on Azure), shifted Office to Office 365 subscriptions. Target of $20bn commercial cloud run-rate by FY18 (from $6.3bn) was beaten in 2017. Market cap >$2tn by 2021, >$3tn by 2024-25; Fool: >1,160% gain since Feb 2014 (2025). Peak ~$555 mid-2025 [unverified] = ~15x plus dividends. Split [approx, my calc]: EPS FY14 ~$2.63 -> FY25 ~$13.6 (~5x); P/E ~14x -> ~35x (~2.5x). Max drawdown: ~-37% in 2022 ($349 -> ~$213). EARLY SIGNAL visible 2014-15: Azure growing >100% y/y, Office 365 consumer/commercial seat growth, deferred revenue rising, a CEO publicly killing the Windows-first culture — while the stock still priced as a declining PC monopoly. Who caught it: ValueAct Capital (Jeff Ubben) built a ~$2bn stake in 2013 and got a board seat (Mason Morfit, 2014) [from memory, unverified in this pass]. Ended/stalled: AI capex surge (2025-26) raised questions about returns; 2026 status not verified here. LESSON: an insider CEO who reallocates capital away from the legacy cash cow toward a recurring-revenue platform can turn a 'value trap' into a 10x+ via both EPS and multiple.

data.early_signals: Azure >100% growth; O365 seats; culture reset; low P/E
data.lesson: new CEO + recurring revenue pivot = EPS + rerating

title: AMD 2014-2025: Lisa Su turnaround, ~$1.6 -> ~$200+
body: Lisa Su became CEO Oct 2014 with AMD near insolvency: ~$2.5bn debt, market cap <$2bn, stock just over $3 on her first day, falling to ~$1.61 (2015-16 low). Plan: exit low-margin businesses, bet the company on one high-performance core (Zen), use console semi-custom chips (PS4/Xbox One) for cash. Zen/Ryzen launched 2017 (+52% IPC claimed); EPYC servers 2017; Zen 3 (2020) took the single-thread lead from Intel. Two external helps: TSMC process (GlobalFoundries quit 7nm 2018) and Intel's 10nm delays. Stock tripled by mid-2016, crossed $100 in 2020, peaked ~$227 (Mar 2024) and ~$260s (Oct 2025 after the OpenAI GPU deal) [2025 peak unverified]; ~140x+ from trough. Split: started loss-making, so the move was earnings creation (EPS from negative to ~$3+ adj) plus P/S from ~0.3x to ~8-10x; classic loss-to-profit turnaround. Drawdowns: ~-67% Nov 2021-Oct 2022; also >-50% in 2018 [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2016: Zen engineering samples matching Intel Broadwell-E in public demos (Dec 2016); debt restructured; gross margin inching up from ~23% to 30%+ [unverified]; insider-led focus. Who caught it: mostly retail and tech growth funds; no single famous value investor documented. Status: market value ~$675-800bn cited 2026; GPU challenge to Nvidia ongoing. LESSON: an engineer-CEO with a single product bet, an outsourced manufacturing edge and a stumbling incumbent can create a 100x from near-bankruptcy; the first proof was a benchmark, not a quarterly EPS.

data.early_signals: Zen demos 2016, console cash, debt restructuring, Intel 10nm delays
data.lesson: engineer-CEO + one product bet + incumbent stumble

title: Tesla 2010-2024: narrative compounder with -73% and -60% drawdowns
body: Split-adjusted (5:1 2020, 3:1 2022 = 15x): IPO June 2010 $17 (~$1.13). June 2019 low just under $177 (~$11.8) amid Model 3 cash fears. Peak Nov 2021 ~$414 (closing ~$410): ~35x in 2.5 years. Then -73% to ~$101 (Jan 2023) on demand worries, price cuts and Musk's Twitter purchase/share sales; -65% in calendar 2022 alone. New high ~$488 (Dec 2024) on robotaxi/policy hopes [unverified]. Split: overwhelmingly rerating — GAAP profits only began 2020; at the 2021 peak the market cap exceeded most automakers combined while P/E was >100x. EPS did grow fast 2020-22, then fell 2023-24 as auto margins collapsed from ~30% to <20% [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible mid/late 2019: Model 3 run-rate ~5k/week sustained, a surprise Q3 2019 profit, Shanghai Gigafactory built in ~10 months — i.e., the existential risk was ending while short interest was extreme. Who caught it: Baron Funds (Ron Baron, long-time holder from ~2014, publicly), ARK Invest (Cathie Wood's 2018 $4,000 pre-split target), Baillie Gifford (early holder, trimmed 2020-22) [holder details from memory, unverified]. Stall: 2024 was the first annual delivery decline; valuation now rests on autonomy/robotics optionality. LESSON: when survival risk resolves in a heavily shorted category-creator, the rerating can be violent; but a price driven mostly by multiple is fragile and swings -60-75% repeatedly.

data.early_signals: Model 3 ramp, Q3 2019 profit, Shanghai plant speed, extreme short interest
data.who_caught_it: Ron Baron, Cathie Wood/ARK, Baillie Gifford [unverified details]
data.lesson: survival-risk resolution rerates; multiple-driven prices are fragile

title: Super Micro 2023-2026: AI-server 17x, then -86% on governance
body: Split-adjusted (10:1, Oct 2024): ~$4-7 in 2022-early 2023 -> intraday ~$122.9 (Mar 2024), joining the S&P 500: ~17-30x [prices from memory, unverified]. Revenue roughly doubled FY23->FY24 (~$7bn -> ~$15bn) on Nvidia GPU server racks and liquid cooling. Then: gross margin fell to 11.3% (June 2024 qtr) from 17%; Hindenburg short report (Aug 27 2024: accounting red flags, related parties, export-control issues); 10-K delayed; Ernst & Young resigned Oct 30 2024 saying it could no longer rely on management/audit-committee representations (-33% day). Low ~$17 (Nov 2024), ~-86% from peak [unverified exact]. BDO hired Nov 2024; overdue reports filed Feb 2025 without restatement, but BDO issued adverse opinions on internal controls. Margins kept sliding (9.3% FQ1'26; 6.4% adj FQ2'26). March 2026: US indicted co-founder Wally Liaw and two others for diverting ~$2.5bn of Nvidia-based servers (~$510m reaching China); stock -33% in a day; company not charged. EARLY RED FLAGS visible before the peak: 2018 Nasdaq delisting for late filings, 2020 SEC accounting settlement (~$17.5m) [unverified], rehiring of executives tied to that episode, related-party suppliers, and falling gross margin while revenue soared (a commoditised assembler). Who caught it: momentum buyers on the way up; Hindenburg on the way down. LESSON: revenue hypergrowth in a low-moat assembler plus a known governance history is a peak-hype setup; margin compression is the first tell.

data.eps_vs_rerating: EPS + rerating up; margin collapse down
data.early_signals: up: AI rack share; down: prior SEC case, 2018 delisting, GM 17%->11%
data.lesson: governance history + commodity margins = fragile multibagger

title: Palantir 2022-2026: ~35x on AIP, mostly multiple, then -36%
body: Direct listing Sept 2020 (~$10). Low ~$6 in late 2022 (all-time low $6.55 by May 2022; ~$5.9 Dec 2022), -87% from the Jan 2021 meme peak (~$45) [peak unverified]. P/S fell from 35x (Sep 2021) to 8.5x (Sep 2022). Then: first GAAP profit Q4 2022 and consecutive profitable quarters (S&P 500 entry Sept 2024); AIP launched 2023 with 'bootcamps' (560 done by Feb 2024) that accelerated US commercial deals; Q1 2026 revenue +85% y/y to $1.633bn. Peak ~$207 (Nov 2025) [unverified] ≈ 35x from the low. P/S hit 137x (Aug 2025, Motley Fool) — the stock outran even 85% growth. Split: overwhelmingly rerating (P/S 8.5x -> 137x ≈ 16x) vs revenue ~2.5x. By Nov 13 2026: ~-36% from ATH, ~60x sales, forward P/E ~85 vs ~200 at peak — multiple compression despite growth. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2023: sustained GAAP profitability (index eligibility), accelerating US commercial customer count and deal size after bootcamps, rule-of-40 score rising, while the stock was at ~8x sales. Who caught it: retail community, Wedbush's Dan Ives, ARK (bought 2022-23) [unverified]. LESSON: real fundamental acceleration started it, but a 16x multiple expansion means future returns depend on keeping hype; Motley Fool notes only 7 other software firms ever traded >100x sales and all fell >=70% from peak valuation.

data.early_signals: GAAP profitability -> S&P eligibility; AIP bootcamps; US commercial acceleration at 8x sales
data.lesson: >100x sales base rate is brutal even with 85% growth

title: Costco 2009-2026: membership flywheel, ~29x with heavy P/E expansion
body: Costco's ~14-15% markup cap and membership fees (which are most of operating profit) create a low-price, high-trust flywheel; renewal rates ~90% US/Canada. March 2009 low ~$38 [unverified] -> all-time high $1,094.32 (May 2026): ~29x plus special dividends ($5 2015, $7 2017, $10 2020, $15 2024) [unverified]. Split [approx]: EPS ~$2.5 (FY09) -> ~$18 (FY25) ≈ 7x; P/E ~15x -> ~48-60x ≈ 3.5x. Feb 2025 P/E ~60x was the highest in its history (prior record 56.4x in Apr 1999, after which the stock fell >20% in months; Aug 2026 trailing ~48x). Drawdowns: ~-50% 2007-09 and after the 1999 valuation peak [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL (always visible): rising paid members, renewal rates, fee increases every ~5-6 years with no churn, comparable sales beating peers through recessions. Who caught it: Charlie Munger (Costco director from 1997, lifelong holder and public advocate); Berkshire held Costco ~2000-2020 and sold in 2020 near ~$300 [from memory, unverified], missing ~3.5x. Stall: by 2025-26 growth ~high single digit at ~50x earnings — commentators flag 'very light growth' for the price. LESSON: a capital-light-ish customer-aligned model compounds EPS steadily; the last decade's extra return came from the market paying up for certainty, which is a non-repeatable tailwind and a risk.

data.early_signals: member count, ~90% renewals, fee hikes without churn
data.lesson: steady EPS + rerating tailwind; Berkshire sold too early

title: Domino's Pizza 2008-2021: 'our pizza was bad' turnaround, ~180x from trough
body: IPO July 2004 at $14. Highly levered (securitised debt), it hit ~$3 in Nov 2008 [unverified] and was in the low single digits in early 2009. Dec 2009: CEO-elect Patrick Doyle (CEO Mar 2010) launched the ~$75m 'Pizza Turnaround' campaign on camera admitting customers found the pizza poor, with a new recipe; same-store sales jumped ~14% in Q1 2010 [unverified]. Then a digital-first strategy (Pizza Tracker 2008, online/app ordering, later >half of US sales digital), store remodels, and a 'fortressing' franchise model. Under Doyle the stock rose ~13x (Restaurant Business); Quartz noted it beat Google's return from 2010. Peak ~$567 (Dec 2021) [unverified] ≈ ~180x from the 2008 low, ~65x from 2010. Split: mostly EPS + aggressive buybacks/recaps (negative equity, share count down); P/E moved from ~10x to ~30x+ [unverified]. Drawdown: ~-80% 2007-08 pre-turnaround [unverified]; -~35% 2022. EARLY SIGNAL visible in 2010: the honest relaunch produced an immediate double-digit same-store-sales jump — a measurable demand response — at a ~10x P/E. Who caught it: few documented; later Berkshire Hathaway disclosed a DPZ stake (Q3 2024). Stall: 2022-26 range-bound as US delivery competition and aggregators matured. LESSON: in a franchise model, a product reset that shows up in same-store sales within one quarter, plus leverage-funded buybacks, can produce a 100x; check the first comp print.

data.early_signals: Q1 2010 same-store sales jump after honest relaunch; digital ordering share
data.lesson: first comp print after product reset is the signal

title: Priceline/Booking 2002-2025: hidden European segment inside a dot-com wreck
body: Priceline fell from ~$974 (1999, adjusted for the 2003 1:6 reverse split) to ~$6.60-7 in Oct 2002 (-99%). CEO Jeffery Boyd and team bought UK Active Hotels (2004) and Dutch Booking.com (2005, ~$133m [unverified]); Booking.com's agency model (hotels pay commission after stay, broad SME hotel supply in Europe) became the profit engine. Fortune (2017): best total shareholder return of any large company over the prior decade; ~3,000% in 10 years to 2015. Reached ~$1,500+ by 2016-17 and ~$5,000-5,800 by 2025 [unverified]: roughly 800x from the 2002 low. Split: mostly EPS growth (gross bookings compounding 20-30% for a decade plus margin expansion and buybacks); P/E stayed ~20-30x [unverified]. Drawdowns: -99% 2000-02; ~-70% 2008 [unverified]; ~-45% 2020 COVID. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2005-07: international gross bookings growing far faster than the US name-your-own-price business and becoming the majority of profit, disclosed in segment data — while the market still saw a damaged US dot-com. Who caught it: few documented names; it was a classic 'hidden segment' that analysts initially underweighted. Stall: post-2018 growth normalised to ~10%, still compounding via buybacks. LESSON: a small acquired segment with platform economics inside an unloved parent can carry the whole valuation; read the segment notes.

data.early_signals: Booking.com/Active Hotels international bookings growth in segment data
data.lesson: hidden segment with platform economics inside a broken parent

title: Meta 2022-2025: $88 trough to ~9x via 'Year of Efficiency'
body: Meta fell ~-77% from Sept 2021 (~$384) to an intraday low $88.09 on Nov 4 2022 (close $90.70) on Apple ATT ad-targeting losses, TikTok, the first revenue declines, ~$10bn+/yr Reality Labs losses and 2023 capex guidance near $40bn. Trough P/E ~9x, lower ex-cash. Oct 24 2022: Altimeter's Brad Gerstner published an open letter urging ~20% headcount cuts, capex cuts and capping metaverse spend at ~$5bn/yr. Nov 2022: 13% layoffs; Feb 1 2023: Zuckerberg declared 2023 the 'Year of Efficiency' with a bigger buyback (stock +23% that day [unverified]); 2023 the stock +178%, its best year. Then AI-driven ad targeting (Advantage+), Reels monetisation and margins back to ~40%+; peak ~$790s (Aug 2025) [unverified] ≈ 9x from the low. Split [approx]: EPS 2022 ~$8.6 -> 2024 ~$23.9 (~2.8x); P/E ~9x -> ~25-28x (~3x). EARLY SIGNAL visible at the trough: daily users still growing (~2bn+ DAP), engagement intact, a founder-controlled company with a cost problem that the founder could switch off, priced like a dying business; Gerstner's letter made the cost lever explicit. Who caught it: Brad Gerstner/Altimeter (documented letter, holder); 13F-tracked hedge funds bought in Q4 2022 [unverified names]. Ended: late-2025 AI capex guidance (>$100bn) pulled the stock back [unverified]. LESSON: a dominant platform at a single-digit ex-cash P/E whose problem is discretionary spending (not demand) is a high-probability turnaround once management signals cost discipline.

data.early_signals: users/engagement intact; spend-driven (not demand) problem; 9x P/E; activist letter
data.lesson: fixable cost problem in a monopoly-like platform at trough multiple

title: Novo Nordisk 2016-2026: GLP-1 category creator, round trip -73%
body: Novo pioneered GLP-1s (Victoza 2010, Ozempic 2017, Wegovy for obesity June 2021). Rise: STEP-1 (Feb 2021, ~15% weight loss), Wegovy launch June 2021 with supply shortages for two years, SELECT (Aug 2023, ~20% fewer heart events). The stock roughly quadrupled from 2021 [approx] and Novo became Europe's most valuable company, worth >$600-650bn at the June 2024 peak — more than Denmark's GDP; ADR ~$145-150 (2:1 split Sep 2023) [unverified]. Mostly EPS growth (sales/EPS growing 20-30%+), with P/E expanding to ~40-45x [unverified]. Reversal: Dec 20 2024 CagriSema trial disappointment -20% (record one-day fall); Lilly's tirzepatide took 63% of US branded obesity scripts by Q3 2025; compounded semaglutide eroded cash pay; CEO Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen ousted May 16 2025 (shares -59% from June 2024 high at that point); new CEO Mike Doustdar cut 9,000 jobs (Sept 2025); Nov 2025 US pricing deal cut government prices; 2026 guidance: first sales decline in modern history (-5% to -13%); Feb 23 2026 CagriSema lost head-to-head vs tirzepatide, -16%, shares at lowest since June 2021 — ~$475bn (~73%) wiped. EARLY SIGNAL (up): Wegovy shortages = demand exceeding supply for 2+ years. EARLY SIGNAL (down): SURPASS/SURMOUNT data showing a better competitor molecule plus Lilly out-investing in capacity, and Novo's next-gen data underwhelming in Dec 2024. LESSON: the category creator does not automatically own the category; peak valuation coincided with peak scarcity, and a superior fast follower plus price normalisation erased the whole Wegovy-era gain.

data.eps_vs_rerating: up: EPS + P/E to ~40x; down: P/E collapse + EPS cuts
data.early_signals: up: Wegovy shortages; down: Lilly superior data, CagriSema miss Dec 2024
data.who_caught_it: broad European/US growth funds; no documented single name
data.lesson: category creator lost to faster follower; peak scarcity = peak price

title: Eli Lilly 2018-2025: better GLP-1 molecule, first $1tn drugmaker
body: Lilly was a mid-sized pharma (~$80-110 in 2018 [unverified]) behind J&J, Pfizer, Merck. Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1): SURPASS-2 (2021) beat semaglutide in diabetes; SURMOUNT-1 (Apr 2022) showed ~21-22% weight loss; Mounjaro approved May 2022, Zepbound (obesity) Nov 2023. 2024 sales: Mounjaro $11.5bn, Zepbound $4.9bn; Q3 2025 Mounjaro $6.5bn (+109%), Zepbound $3.6bn (+185%). Lilly took ~63% of US branded obesity scripts by Q3 2025 and invested tens of billions in manufacturing capacity. Nov 21 2025: first drugmaker to a $1tn market value (~$1,050+/share [unverified]) — ~10-13x from 2018; +75% since Zepbound launch vs S&P +50%; ~50x forward earnings. Split: EPS grew several-fold 2022-25 but P/E also expanded from ~20x to ~50x [approx]. Drawdown: ~-30%+ between Aug 2024 high and mid-2025 on oral-pill data and pricing worries [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2021-22: head-to-head data beating the market leader's molecule (SURPASS-2), then SURMOUNT-1's weight-loss magnitude — public, peer-reviewed, before revenue. Who caught it: broad healthcare growth funds; no single documented investor found. Risks: price cuts under US government deals, orforglipron/oral competition, Novo/new entrants. LESSON: in category creation the winner is often the best-data fast follower with manufacturing scale, not the pioneer; head-to-head trial data is the early public signal.

data.early_signals: SURPASS-2 head-to-head win 2021; SURMOUNT-1 2022
data.lesson: best-data fast follower + capacity wins the category

title: ASML 2012-2024: EUV monopoly co-funded by its customers, ~22x
body: July-Sept 2012: Intel, TSMC and Samsung took a combined 23% stake in ASML for €3.85bn and committed €1.38bn to EUV and 450mm R&D (customer co-investment program; Intel ~15%, TSMC 5%, Samsung 3%). ASML also bought Cymer (light source) in 2012-13. EUV took until ~2017-19 to reach volume production; ASML is the only supplier, enabling 7nm and below. ADR ~$49 (July 2012, Intel investment date) -> ~$172 (Oct 2018, +350%) -> peak ~$1,100 (July 2024) [unverified] ≈ 22x plus dividends. Split [approx]: EPS ~€2.6 (2012) -> ~€19 (2024) ≈ 7x; P/E ~20x -> ~40x ≈ 2x. Drawdowns: ~-59% (Nov 2021-Oct 2022) and ~-45-50% (July 2024-2025) on China export curbs and order softness [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible in 2012: the three largest chipmakers paying billions for equity to make sure EUV got built — customers voting with capital for a single-source chokepoint. Samsung's retained stake reportedly grew ~17x. Who caught it: the customers themselves (TSMC sold out 2015, Intel/Samsung trimmed from 2016 — leaving most of the gain on the table). LESSON: when customers co-fund a supplier's monopoly technology, the moat is being built in public; the payoff took 5-7 years of technical risk and the stock stays cyclical (-50% swings) even as a monopoly.

data.early_signals: Intel/TSMC/Samsung €3.85bn equity co-investment for EUV
data.who_caught_it: customers (Intel, TSMC, Samsung) — most sold early
data.lesson: customer co-investment = public moat signal; monopolies stay cyclical

title: TSMC 2012-2026: foundry scale + AI, ADR ~$15 -> $363, $2tn
body: TSMC's pure-foundry model (never competing with customers) plus relentless capex created a process lead once Intel's 10nm/7nm slipped (2016-20) and GlobalFoundries quit 7nm (2018). Apple A-series exclusivity (from ~A10, 2016, helped by InFO packaging) and then Nvidia/AMD AI accelerators (CoWoS advanced packaging) concentrated leading-edge demand on TSMC; gross margins >50%. ADR ~$15 in 2012 [unverified] -> record $319.61 (Jan 2026, $1.66tn) -> crossed $2tn market cap Feb 24 2026 -> record ~$363 (Apr 2026): ~24x plus dividends. Split: mostly EPS growth; P/E moved from ~12-15x to ~25-30x [approx]. Drawdown: ~-58% (Jan-Oct 2022) on cycle + Taiwan risk. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2017-19: Intel publicly delaying 10nm while TSMC shipped 7nm on schedule with Apple/AMD/Huawei; capex guidance rising faster than peers'; rising gross margin despite heavy depreciation. Who caught it / famous miss: Berkshire bought ~$4bn of ADRs in Q3 2022 near the low and sold almost all within a quarter, Buffett citing geopolitical risk [from memory, unverified in this pass]. LESSON: scale-driven manufacturing monopolies compound through cycles; the 'geopolitical discount' kept the P/E low for a decade and was itself the opportunity for those who could size for tail risk.

data.early_signals: Intel 10nm delays vs TSMC 7nm on time; Apple exclusivity; rising capex
data.lesson: manufacturing scale moat; geopolitical discount as opportunity, size for tail

title: Hermès and LVMH 2009-2025: luxury pricing power, then the China reversal
body: From the 2009 trough, both compounded on Chinese wealth creation, price increases above inflation and supply-limited products (Birkin waitlists; Louis Vuitton never discounts). Hermès: ~€90 (2009) [unverified] -> ~€2,750 (Feb 2025) ≈ 30x; operating margin ~40%. LVMH: ~€40 (Mar 2009) [unverified] -> ~€900 (Apr 2023) ≈ 22x; Bernard Arnault briefly became world's richest. Split: mostly EPS (sales and margins up), plus P/E expansion to ~50x for Hermès and ~25-30x for LVMH [approx]. Side story: LVMH secretly built a ~17-23% Hermès stake via equity swaps (2010), fined by the AMF and distributed in 2014 — Hermès family formed a holding to lock control [from memory, unverified]. Reversal: May 2023 one-day $30bn luxury sell-off on US/China demand fears; China reopening bet faded; 2024 was a bad year for LVMH/Kering (Hermès held up); by Sept 2026 LVMH ~-55% from its 2023 peak (~-37% in 2026), out of Europe's top 10; Hermès down to ~€1,382 from ~€2,750 (date of quote unverified). EARLY SIGNAL visible ~2009-12: double-digit organic growth in Asia, price increases without volume loss, waitlists — pricing power. Who caught it: family owners (Arnault, Dumas/Puech); no documented outside name. LESSON: premiumisation compounders still carry demand cycles; Hermès (scarcity) held far better than LVMH (breadth) when the China aspirational buyer retreated, and a 50x P/E leaves no cushion.

data.early_signals: price hikes w/o volume loss, waitlists, Asian organic growth
data.lesson: scarcity beats breadth in luxury downturns; luxury is still cyclical

title: Constellation Software 2006-2025: serial VMS acquirer ~300x, then -50%
body: Founded 1995 by ex-VC Mark Leonard; IPO on TSX May 2006 (~C$17.50 [unverified]). Model: buy hundreds of small vertical-market software (VMS) firms at low multiples with strict hurdle rates, keep them decentralised, reinvest all cash flow; Leonard's letters reported ROIC and organic growth candidly and set the playbook (later spun-offs Topicus, Lumine). Peak ~C$5,000-5,300 (2025) [unverified] ≈ 300x + dividends. Split: almost entirely FCF/share growth; P/E/FCF multiple also rose from ~10-15x to ~30x+ [approx]. Drawdowns: ~-35-40% in 2008 [unverified]; then the big one: Sept 25 2025 Leonard resigned for health reasons (Mark Miller president), shares closed the week -17% days after an investor call on AI worries; National Bank downgraded; AI-disruption fear hit all SaaS/VMS; by Feb 2026 ~-51% from highs, 52-week low ~C$2,624 (Jan 2026), ~16-17x forward earnings by mid-2026. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2006-2012: shareholder letters showing high returns on many small, boring acquisitions, a growing count of deals per year, and owner-operator incentives (managers required to buy shares with bonus). Who caught it: early backers OMERS/Ontario pension funds; a cult following of quality investors [names unverified]. LESSON: capital-allocation compounders depend on the allocator and on the redeployment runway; key-person exit + a new technology threat can halve even a 300x stock without any fundamental miss yet.

data.early_signals: letters showing high ROIC on small VMS deals; owner incentives
data.lesson: key-person + runway risk in serial acquirers

title: MercadoLibre 2007-2025: LatAm marketplace + fintech, ~130x with -88% and -67% crashes
body: IPO Aug 10 2007 at $18 (first-day ~$27.62). Fell ~-88% in 2008 [unverified exact] amid the GFC and LatAm FX. Built Mercado Pago (payments, launched for marketplace buyers lacking cards/trust; later wallets, credit, merchant acquiring), Mercado Envios logistics (2013+) and ads. Stock ~$2,330 in Aug 2025 (+12,844% ≈ 130x since IPO, Motley Fool), peak ~$2,600 in 2025 [unverified]; ~$1,886 close on July 30 2026 (+6,728% vs first-day price). Split: mostly revenue/EPS growth (profitability arrived late, ~2020+); valuation stayed high on P/S. Drawdowns: ~-88% (2007-08); ~-67% (2021-22, ~$1,970 -> ~$600) [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible ~2010-17: Mercado Pago total payment volume growing faster than marketplace GMV, increasingly off-platform — a fintech hidden inside an e-commerce stock; eBay had held ~19% from 2001 [unverified]. Who caught it: Baillie Gifford and other long-term growth funds [unverified in this pass]. Status: 2026 pullback on credit-book provisioning and competition (Shopee, Temu, Amazon) [unverified]. LESSON: in underpenetrated regions, the platform that also solves payments, logistics and trust builds a multi-sided moat; expect EM-style -70-90% drawdowns along the way.

data.early_signals: Mercado Pago TPV outgrowing GMV; logistics build
data.lesson: multi-sided EM platform solving payments+logistics; survive EM drawdowns

title: Axon (ex-TASER) 2017-2025: hardware to public-safety SaaS, ~35x
body: TASER International renamed itself Axon in April 2017 (after its body-camera and Evidence.com cloud unit) and offered every US police department free body cameras and a year of cloud storage — converting one-time hardware sales into multi-year subscription bundles (cameras + TASER + cloud + later Fusus, drones, AI report-writing 'Draft One'). Founder-CEO Rick Smith got a 2018 market-cap-milestone award. Stock ~$24 (2017 rebrand) [unverified] -> 52-week highs ~$800-880 in 2025 [unverified] ≈ 35x; +600% since 2020 per 2025 coverage. ARR $1.2bn (Q2 2025) from $850m a year earlier; Q4 2025 revenue +39% to $797m; stock +16-17% on Q2 2025 and Q4 2025 prints. Only ~30% of customers on premium plans (Q4 2025) = upsell runway. Split: largely rerating (EV/sales from ~4x to ~20x+) on a recurring-revenue mix shift, plus revenue ~6x [approx]. Drawdown: ~-50% in 2021-22 [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2017-19: the free-camera land-grab, rising Evidence.com seats and multi-year bookings (RPO) disclosed each quarter, gross margin rising as software mix grew. Who caught it: growth funds; no single documented name found. LESSON: a hardware incumbent that gives away the device to lock in software subscriptions in a sticky government market can rerate from hardware to SaaS multiples; watch ARR and RPO, not unit sales.

data.early_signals: free body-camera offer; Evidence.com seats; RPO growth; GM rising
data.lesson: razor/blade to SaaS in sticky gov market; track ARR/RPO

title: Celsius 2020-2025: Pepsi-distribution 60x+, then -73% on destocking
body: Split-adjusted (3:1, Nov 2023): ~$1-1.5 in early 2020 [unverified] -> ~$99 (Mar-May 2024; YTD high $98.72 in May): ~60-70x. Driver: 'better-for-you' fitness energy drink sold to young women/gym users, then the Aug 2022 PepsiCo long-term US distribution deal (Pepsi invested ~$550m for ~8.5% [unverified]) that put Celsius in Pepsi's DSD network nationwide; revenue roughly tripled 2022-23 [unverified]. Mostly revenue/EPS growth, but P/E also peaked near 100x [unverified]. Reversal: Pepsi had over-ordered and then destocked — Q3 2024 revenue -31% to $266m, net income -92% — while retail scanner sales still grew ~7%; Alani Nu, Ghost and others took share; stock -73% (May-Sept 2024 to ~$32), -52% in 2024, low ~$21 early 2025 [unverified]. Feb 2025: bought Alani Nu for $1.8bn (cash + $500m stock), stock +~20-30%; closed Apr 1 2025. EARLY SIGNAL (up): distribution step-change into a national DSD system, measured in scanner data before reported revenue. EARLY SIGNAL (down): reported revenue running far ahead of scanner sell-through in 2023-24 — distributor inventory build. Who caught it: retail/momentum; no documented famous name. LESSON: a distribution deal gives a one-time step change; when sell-in (reported sales) outruns sell-through (scanner data), the destocking reversal is predictable — a direct echo of Monster's playbook but at a much higher price.

data.early_signals: up: Pepsi DSD deal 2022; down: sell-in > scanner sell-through
data.lesson: distribution step change is one-time; monitor scanner vs reported sales

title: Shopify 2015-2025: ~100x, -87% crash, recovery to new highs
body: IPO May 2015 at $17 (10:1 split June 2022 -> ~$1.70). Rose ~6,480% to the Nov 2021 peak (~$169-176 split-adj) as the 'arms dealer' to independent merchants; Merchant Solutions (Shopify Payments, Capital, Shipping) overtook subscriptions — take-rate on GMV, not seats. Crash: 2022 bear market + post-COVID e-commerce normalisation + a capex-heavy logistics push (Deliverr bought for $2.1bn in 2022) returned Shopify to losses; stock -87% to $23.63 (Sept 2022). Reset: 10% layoffs July 2022, then May 2023 20% layoffs and sale of logistics/Deliverr to Flexport for a ~13% stake; stock +27% that day. Back to asset-light: positive operating income for 9+ quarters, FCF margins mid-teens+ [unverified]. New all-time high in late Oct 2025 (surpassing 2021; C$253 on TSX); 2025 was described as its best year. Split: 2015-21 mostly multiple on fast revenue; 2023-25 mostly margins/FCF growth. EARLY SIGNAL visible 2016-18: Payments attach rate rising, Plus enterprise merchants, app-ecosystem revenue — platform economics; in 2023 the signal was management abandoning capex-heavy logistics. Who caught it: founder Tobi Lütke (controlling shares); Baillie Gifford and other growth funds [unverified]. LESSON: a platform that drifts into capital-intensive operations loses its multiple; reversing that drift is itself a buy signal, and recovery to new highs took ~4 years.

data.early_signals: payments attach, Merchant Solutions > subscriptions; 2023 logistics exit
data.lesson: platforms lose multiple when they go capital-heavy; reversal is the signal

title: Enphase 2016-2025: near-bankrupt to ~400x, then -90% bust
body: Microinverter maker trading below ~$1 in 2016-17 with going-concern-type worries [unverified]. Badri Kothandaraman (COO 2017, CEO Sept 2017) ran a cost/pricing/opex plan: redesigned IQ microinverters, cut costs, raised prices, refinanced debt; gross margin from ~20% to ~40%+ [unverified]. Joined S&P 500 Jan 2021. Peak ~$340 (Dec 2022) [unverified] ≈ 400x from the low. Split: loss-to-profit plus P/E up to ~100x; US residential solar boom (30% 25D tax credit, IRA 2022), California NEM 2.0. Bust: California NEM 3.0 (Apr 2023) cut payback economics, rates rose (solar loans), European distributor inventory glut 2023-24, SolarEdge-style channel destock; then the July 2025 tax law phased out the 25D credit for customer-owned systems after 2025. Stock $40.47 mid-2025 (-67% from Aug 2024's $123.65), ~$30s late 2025: ~-90% from peak [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL (up) visible 2018: gross margin rising quarter after quarter with a new CEO's public 3-step plan, while the stock was <$5. EARLY SIGNAL (down): demand dependent on one state's net-metering rule and federal credits, plus distributor inventory rising faster than installs. Who caught it: few documented; retail/momentum. LESSON: a genuine operational turnaround can ride a policy-subsidised boom to 400x, but demand that exists because of subsidies reverses when policy and rates turn; treat as cyclical, not compounder.

data.early_signals: up: GM expansion under new CEO; down: NEM 3.0, rates, channel inventory, 25D phase-out
data.lesson: subsidy-driven demand is cyclical; policy is the hidden variable

title: Amazon 1997-2021: ~2,500x via FCF per share, through a -94% crash
body: IPO May 1997 at $18. Splits 2:1 (1998), 3:1 (1999), 2:1 (1999), 20:1 (2022) = 240x: IPO ≈ $0.075 on today's basis. Dot-com peak Dec 1999 ~$107 nominal (~$4.4 adj) -> Sept 2001 ~$5.5 (~$0.28 adj): -94%. July 2021 peak ~$3,770 pre-2022-split (~$188): ~2,500x from IPO; ~670x from the 2001 low [split math mine]. Split: EPS was near-zero/negative for years by design; the driver was operating cash flow and later AWS profits; P/E is not meaningful. EARLY SIGNAL visible 1997-2002: the 1997 shareholder letter ('It's all about the long term', optimise for FCF per share, not GAAP EPS), negative working-capital cycle (paid by customers before paying suppliers), and customer counts compounding; Prime (2005) and AWS (2006) were later hidden segments — AWS was first broken out only in 2015, revealing a highly profitable cloud business. Who caught it: Bill Miller (Legg Mason) bought at the IPO, re-entered ~$88 pre-split in the late 1990s, and doubled down near ~$6 in 2001 after a -93% fall, reasoning the book business generated FCF with little inventory risk (247wallst); Nick Sleep/Qais Zakaria (Nomad, from ~2005) [unverified]. Ended/stalled: 2021 peak then -56% in 2022 (see case_study:amazon-drawdown). LESSON: the right metric can differ from EPS (FCF/share, unit economics); a founder willing to reinvest at scale and a hidden segment (AWS) can deliver 1,000x+, but only to holders who survive a -94% drawdown.

data.early_signals: 1997 letter (FCF/share focus), negative working capital, customer growth; AWS disclosure 2015
data.who_caught_it: Bill Miller (doubled down ~$6 in 2001); Nick Sleep/Nomad [unverified]
data.lesson: right metric + founder reinvestment + hidden segment; survive -94%

title: Turnarounds under a new CEO: the first proof print is the signal
body: Cases: Microsoft (Nadella 2014, $36 -> ~15x), AMD (Su 2014, ~$1.6 -> ~140x), Domino's (Doyle 2010, ~13x under him), Enphase (Kothandaraman 2017, ~400x then -90%), Meta (founder self-reset 2022-23, ~9x), Apple (Jobs 1997, then 2003-12 ~110x). Common pattern: (1) the stock is priced as a declining or dying business — P/E 9-15x or P/S <1x, often near-bankrupt; (2) the new leader publicly kills a sacred cow (Windows-first, low-margin segments, the old recipe, metaverse spending) and names a few measurable targets; (3) a single verifiable proof point appears early — Azure >100% growth, Zen benchmark demos, a +14% same-store-sales quarter, quarter-after-quarter gross-margin gains, an opex cut with a buyback; (4) returns come first from survival/rerating, then from EPS. Failure modes: Enphase shows a real operational turnaround can be overwhelmed by policy/cycle; turnaround investors should still ask whether demand is structural. Process rule for memory: don't buy the announcement; buy (or size up) after the first proof print, when the price usually still reflects the old narrative. Expected drawdowns even after the turn: -35% to -67% (MSFT 2022, AMD 2022).

data.signal: first measurable proof point after a public strategy reset

title: Platform economics: take-rate on a growing network beats selling units
body: Cases: Amazon (~2,500x 1997-2021), Booking (~800x from 2002), MercadoLibre (~130x since IPO), Netflix (~1,000x), Shopify (~100x to 2021), Meta (~9x from trough), Apple 2016-23 (Services toll on installed base), Axon (hardware -> SaaS). Shared mechanics: each additional user/merchant/supplier makes the service more valuable to the others; revenue scales as a take-rate on GMV/bookings/engagement rather than as units; incremental margins are high so EPS lags then explodes. Visible early signals: payments or ads attach rising (Shopify Payments, Mercado Pago TPV outgrowing GMV), a segment growing much faster than the parent (Booking.com inside Priceline, AWS inside Amazon), engagement intact while price collapses (Netflix 2011/2022, Meta 2022). Failure mode: platforms that drift into capital-heavy operations lose their multiple (Shopify logistics 2022) and win it back when they exit (2023 Flexport sale). Platforms still suffer -75% to -94% drawdowns; the edge is distinguishing a broken stock from a broken network.

data.signal: attach/take-rate rising; engagement intact during price crash

title: Capital-light compounding: long runways, owner-managers, low capex
body: Cases: Monster (outsourced bottling + distributors; best US stock of 30 years, ~+200,000%), Costco (membership fees ~ most of profit; ~29x since 2009), Constellation Software (~300x via small VMS acquisitions funded by FCF), Domino's (franchise; ~180x from trough), Hermès (scarcity pricing; ~30x), Booking (agency model). Shared traits: high returns on incremental capital, someone else funds the assets (co-packers, franchisees, suppliers via negative working capital, customers via membership fees), long-tenured owner-managers (Sacks/Schlosberg, Munger's influence, Leonard, Dumas family), and EPS growth doing most of the work for a decade or more. Early signals: rising gross margin with flat capex, renewal/retention data, management letters reporting ROIC honestly. Where they stall: (1) key-person exit plus a new threat (Constellation -51% after Leonard left + AI fears); (2) the multiple gets ahead of growth (Costco ~50-60x on high-single-digit growth; Hermès ~50x before a ~-50% fall); (3) growth slows to GDP-plus (Monster 2022-24, Domino's 2022-26). Lesson: these are the best 'hold forever' candidates, but late-stage returns depend on entry multiple; a P/E doubling in the last stretch is a non-repeatable gift.

data.signal: GM up, capex flat, high renewal, owner-operators

title: Category creation (GLP-1-type): the pioneer does not automatically win
body: Cases: Novo Nordisk (GLP-1 pioneer; Europe's most valuable company June 2024, then -73% to below pre-Wegovy levels by Feb 2026), Eli Lilly (fast follower with a better molecule; first $1tn drugmaker Nov 2025, ~63% of US branded obesity scripts), Monster (created a category and kept it), Celsius (new sub-category, 60x then -73%), Tesla (EVs; 35x then -73%), Nvidia (AI compute; see case_study:nvidia). Pattern: (1) the up-move begins when demand visibly exceeds supply (Wegovy shortages 2021-23, Model 3 waitlists, Pepsi DSD shelf space) — the signal is scarcity; (2) peak valuation tends to coincide with peak scarcity, exactly when competitors and capacity are arriving; (3) the winner is the player with the best head-to-head data/product and manufacturing/distribution scale (Lilly's SURPASS-2 and capacity spend; Monster's distribution system), not the first mover; (4) price normalisation (US government drug-price deals, compounding, EV price cuts) compresses margins at the same time as share loss. Early warning for the incumbent: a public head-to-head trial or benchmark that shows a superior rival, and its own next-gen product underwhelming (CagriSema Dec 2024). Lesson: in a new category, re-underwrite on competitive data every year; scarcity premiums are temporary.

data.signal_down: superior rival data; own next-gen miss; price normalisation

title: Peak-hype reversals: the tells that preceded -70% to -90% falls
body: Cases and declines: Super Micro (-86%, 2024), Enphase (~-90%, 2022-25), Celsius (-73%, 2024), Tesla (-73%, 2021-23), Shopify (-87%, 2021-22), Palantir (-87% 2021-22; -36% from Nov 2025 peak while growing 85%), Novo (-73%, 2024-26), Constellation (-51%, 2025-26). Recurring tells visible before or at the top: (1) valuation extremes — P/S >30-100x (Palantir 137x; only 7 other software firms ever exceeded 100x sales and all fell >=70%), P/E ~100x (Celsius, Enphase); (2) gross-margin compression while revenue soars (SMCI 17% -> 11% -> 6%); (3) sell-in outrunning sell-through / distributor inventory build (Celsius-Pepsi, Enphase Europe); (4) demand dependent on a subsidy or rule (Enphase: NEM 3.0, 25D credit); (5) governance history (SMCI's 2018 delisting, prior SEC case; auditor resignation as the final alarm); (6) capex-heavy diversification by an asset-light company (Shopify logistics); (7) peak scarcity in a new category (Novo). Note: in most cases the business stayed real — the loss came from price paid and from one fragile assumption. Process rule: when two or more tells co-occur, cut size or require a much lower entry; never average down after an auditor resigns.

title: Great businesses crash -75% too: separate the broken stock from the broken business
body: Every long-run winner in this library had at least one deep drawdown: Amazon -94% (1999-2001), Booking -99% (2000-02), MercadoLibre ~-88% (2008) and ~-67% (2021-22), Netflix ~-80% (2011-12) and -76% (2021-22), Shopify -87% (2022), Meta -77% (2021-22), Palantir -87% (2021-22), Apple -61% (2007-09) and -44% (2012-13), Microsoft -37% (2022), AMD -67% (2021-22), TSMC -58% (2022), ASML -59% (2021-22). Recovery signal that was visible at the bottom in the cases that recovered: core engagement/usage metrics kept growing (Netflix streaming hours, Meta daily users, MELI payments volume) and the cause was management choices or macro, not loss of the moat; management then made a visible reversal (Netflix dropping Qwikster, Meta's efficiency cuts, Shopify selling logistics). Non-recoveries in this set (SMCI, Enphase, Novo so far) had moat or governance problems instead: commodity margins, subsidy-dependent demand, or a superior competitor. Practical rules: size positions so a -75% move is survivable (see strategy:position-sizing); write down in advance which usage metric would prove the business, not the stock, is broken.

data.rule: track usage metric vs price; size for -75%

title: Chokepoint monopolies: customers co-invest, the market under-prices for years
body: Cases: ASML (only EUV supplier; ~22x 2012-24), TSMC (leading-edge foundry; ADR ~24x to $363 and a $2tn market cap by 2026), Nvidia (AI compute; see case_study:nvidia). Pattern: the moat is built in public over 5-10 years of technical risk. Early signals: customers paying to secure supply (Intel/TSMC/Samsung €3.85bn for 23% of ASML in 2012; hyperscalers pre-paying for capacity), competitors publicly slipping (Intel 10nm delays 2016-20, GlobalFoundries exiting 7nm 2018), and rising gross margin despite heavy capex/depreciation. Why under-priced: cyclicality (each still fell -55-60% in 2022), concentration on few customers, and geopolitics (TSMC's Taiwan discount; ASML's China export limits). Notable misses: the strategic investors sold early (TSMC sold its ASML stake in 2015; Intel and Samsung trimmed from 2016), and Berkshire reportedly bought and quickly sold TSMC in 2022 on geopolitical risk [unverified]. Lesson: monopolies at technological chokepoints can be owned through cycles, but size them so the tail risk (export bans, Taiwan) is survivable; buy in the cyclical drawdowns, not at AI-peak multiples.

data.signal: customer co-investment; rival process slips; GM up with capex

title: EPS growth vs P/E rerating: which engine drove the multiple decides durability
body: Decomposing the moves [approximate, my arithmetic from public EPS/P/E ranges]: Apple 2003-12 ~110x was ~100% EPS with P/E compression; Apple 2016-23 ~8x was ~half EPS (x2.9, buyback-aided) and half P/E (11x -> 30x); Microsoft 2014-25 ~15x = EPS ~5x x P/E ~2.5x; Costco 2009-26 ~29x = EPS ~7x x P/E ~3.5x; Meta 2022-25 ~9x = EPS ~2.8x x P/E ~3x; Palantir 2022-25 ~35x was mostly multiple (P/S 8.5x -> 137x vs revenue ~2.5x); Tesla 2019-21 ~35x was mostly multiple. Durability followed the mix: EPS-led winners kept compounding or stalled gently; multiple-led winners gave back 36-73% (Palantir, Tesla, Celsius, Enphase) even while still growing. The best risk/reward combos had both engines starting from a depressed multiple (the twin-engine pattern: Apple 2016 at ~10x, Meta 2022 at ~9x, Microsoft 2014 at ~14x). Lesson: estimate what share of the expected return requires the multiple to rise; above ~50% from an already-high multiple, the position is a bet on sentiment and should be sized as such.
